1460-the-black-dwarf:
Walter Scott's tale, told by Jedediah Cleishbotham as a Tale of My Landlord, follows the Black Dwarf, a misshapen hermit of the Border hills who aids lovers and thwarts villains in secret. Set amid Jacobite plots and Border feuds, the story links a dwarf's charity to the fate of a young heir and his bride.

Through moorland meetings, disguised identities, and a wedding threatened by conspiracy, Scott mixes folklore with history. The dwarf himself, Elshie, proves more human than legend allows. It is a short, atmospheric Scott romance, best loved for its lonely hero and its Border setting.
24901-the-american-type-of-isthmian-cana:
Senator John Fairfield Dryden gave this speech in the United States Senate on June 14, 1906, on the American type of isthmian canal. The Prudential reprinted it in 1915 among its Panama-Pacific Exposition memorial volumes, honoring Dryden, the company's founder, with a bronze statue at its Newark home office.

Dryden, of the Senate Committee on Interoceanic Canals, backed the lock-level plan for Panama. It stood against the sea-level plan that most of his fellow conferees and an international board of engineers favored at first. His speech defends American engineers, the Isthmian Commission, and Chief Engineer Stevens. The pamphlet records a key turn in how the Panama Canal was built.
31890-song-surf:
Cale Young Rice's 1910 poetry collection Song-Surf was published by Doubleday, Page and Company in September 1910 and dedicated to his sisters. It follows earlier books such as Nirvana Days, Yolanda of Cyprus, and A Night in Avignon. Its contents include With Omar, Jael, To the Sea, The Day-Moon, A Sea-Ghost, The Cry of Eve, and Mary at Nazareth.

Later poems reach the Indus, a Japanese mother, the dead gods, Tintern Abbey, and songs to A. H. R. on love and childhood. Readers get a varied book of lyric verse, classical and romantic in turn, by a Kentucky poet once widely read and now little remembered.
britannica-1911-bergedorf:
Bergedorf is a town of Germany in the territory of Hamburg, on the river Bille, ten miles east by south of the city by rail. It counted 23,728 people in 1900. Vegetables and fruit grown there feed the Hamburg markets, and tanning, glass-making, brewing and brick-making go on in the town.

Bergedorf won civic rights in 1275. From 1420 to 1868 it belonged jointly to Lübeck and Hamburg, a shared lordship that lasted over four centuries. Hamburg then bought it outright. The country round it, the Vierlande, is rich marshland split into four districts, and its fertility explains the market gardens that supply the great port city next door.
britannica-1911-gorbersdorf:
Gorbersdorf is a village and climatic health resort of Germany, in the Prussian province of Silesia. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it in a deep, well-wooded valley of the Waldenburg range, 1,900 feet above the sea. It lies 60 miles south-west of Breslau by rail, and three miles from the Austrian frontier.

Its population is only 700, but it holds four large sanatoria for consumptives. The earliest of them was founded in 1854 by Hermann Brehmer, whose dates the entry gives as 1826-1889. That founding is the village's claim to notice: a small Silesian valley place built into a centre for the open-air treatment of consumption. The whole entry is a short resort notice, giving setting, height, distance and the four sanatoria in a handful of lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-rebd:
Henry of Rebdorf is not a historical personage at all, but a name attached by error to a chronicle of empire and papacy spanning the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. The only link to Rebdorf near Eichstätt is that its first editor published it from a manuscript preserved there, now in Paris, while other copies exist at Neuburg and Vienna. Its title, Chronica or Annales Imperatorum et Paparum, covers events from 1294 to 1362 in two parts.

The first part continues the Flores Temporum of a Swabian Franciscan to 1343 and was probably compiled about 1346 by an unknown writer. The second part, covering 1343 to 1363, was written by Heinrich Taub, called the Deaf, chaplain at St. Willibald's in Eichstätt, who died about 1364 and is known to have journeyed to Rome for the jubilee indulgence in 1350 and admired the crown jewels at Nuremberg in 1361. The chronicle's second part has real historical importance.
doe-osti-3017157-nrel-s-1mw-water-electr:
Nancy Dowe and Kevin Harrison of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory gave these slides at the KIT International Energy Symposium on June 26, 2025. They describe the laboratory's one-megawatt water electrolysis test system at its Energy Systems Integration Facility. Industry stacks are validated there before pilot-scale renewable natural gas production. Renewable natural gas is methane made from captured carbon and green hydrogen.

Validation runs typically last 1,000 hours of continuous, unattended operation, with up to 5,000 hours possible. A run moves through break-in, polarization scans, water sampling, durability periods, and steady-state holds. The one-megawatt system runs at 250 volts and 4,000 amps direct current, limiting stacks to about 125 cells. A 2025 power supply upgrade raised the ceiling to 6,000 amps. The slides also tour biomethanation projects, where microbes turn hydrogen and carbon dioxide into methane.
doe-osti-3366481-rf-digitizer-for-eic-ll:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229755-2026-TECH describes an RF digitizer for the Electron-Ion Collider's low-level radio frequency system. Samson Mai wrote it with Ramakrishna Bachimanchi of Jefferson Lab and Kyle Fahey, Kevin Mernick, and Arshdeep Singh. The collider will reuse the tunnel of the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider, which shuts down in fiscal 2026. The digitizer samples cavity signals so controllers can hold the accelerating field steady.

Firmware and software were developed and validated on a RHIC 197-megahertz cavity during the second quarter of 2026, setting the baseline. Preliminary data show phase noise performance significantly better than the existing RHIC low-level RF system. Cleaner phase measurement means tighter field control for the new collider's beams. The note records the design and first test evidence.
doe-osti-3625659-dune-validating-neutrin: Fermilab note FERMILAB-FN-1299-STUDENT is a one-page internship summary by Andre Vershaw, with Minerba Betancourt named as mentor. Vershaw took part through SULI and Aurora University. The work checks simulated data for DUNE, which will beam neutrinos from Illinois to South Dakota. Vershaw wrote software to study mock detector data and plot trends in it. Early checks found duplicated reconstructed tracks, sharp spikes in the data, and odd energy gaps between interaction types. Those checks guard against simulation changes that quietly harm reconstruction.
doe-osti-3991169-calculating-obukhov-len:
Matthew Kyle Huckins, Cole Daniel Johnson, and Sara Brambilla of Los Alamos National Laboratory work out a formula for the Monin–Obukhov length from standard weather model output. Their report, LA-UR-26-28474, was issued September 22, 2026. The length is a key yardstick for how steady or turbulent the air near the ground is.

Most textbook forms count only the heat rising from the surface. The authors show that water vapor flux matters too, and they fold both fluxes into one working equation. The test case uses fields from the HRRR weather model, but the inputs are common ones: air heat and moisture near the ground, surface pressure, friction speed, and the two heat fluxes. Smoke and plume modelers, who need this yardstick to spread a plume right, get a fuller recipe than the standard one.
nasa-tm-19660006377-some-aspects-of-nois:
Gordon C Augason of the Space Sciences Division, with a colleague from the Instrumentation Division at Ames, analyzes noise in a kind of spectrometer that builds its spectrum in an unusual way. An interferometer spectrometer first records a pattern called an interferogram. A Fourier transform then turns that pattern into a spectrum. Noise in the pattern spreads through the result in ways that need care.

The authors use sampling theory and statistics to work out that spread. They then compare such instruments with conventional spectrometers on noise. Their check confirms a known gain, called Fellgett's advantage, for detectors not limited by background. The paper gives instrument builders a firmer basis for choosing between the two designs.
stifter-das-haidedorf:
A heath, a village, and the quiet lives between them fill Adalbert Stifter's early tale Das Haidedorf, given here in German. The Heath Village portrays rural Austrian life with his unmatched eye for landscape. Nothing loud happens, and that is precisely the point of Stifter's art.

He finds the extraordinary inside the ordinary: weather over the heath, work in the fields, a life unfolding at walking pace. Almost religious attention dignifies every scene he touches. Readers raised on faster fiction may need a page or two to slow down to his rhythm. The reward is a calm few modern writers can match. The tale makes a gentle introduction to a great and demanding author.
the-black-dwarf:
Sir Walter Scott's tale is presented inside a frame called Tales of My Landlord, collected by Jedediah Cleishbotham. That schoolmaster and parish clerk of Gandercleugh introduces himself at length. Contents separate his introduction, an introduction to the tale itself, and the main text.

Cleishbotham argues that Gandercleugh sits at the navel of Scotland, on routes between Edinburgh and Glasgow. Travellers rest at its Wallace Inn, where he has sat by the fire for forty years of evenings. From such talk, he implies, tales are gathered. Envy of merit, learning, and narrow local views are answered in a comic, self-important voice.
